analysis.one_liner: Bans manufacture and sale of semiautomatic assault weapons and large-capacity magazines; current owners keep theirs.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: after winning 149 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, it sat in the Judiciary Committee and its crime subcommittee until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess semiautomatic assault weapons and ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds. People who already owned these guns or magazines when the bill passed could keep them: assault weapons would have to be stored securely and sold only through a licensed dealer with a background check, and existing large magazines could be kept but never resold. Hunting and sporting rifles and shotguns listed in a long exempt appendix, along with bolt-action, pump, and lever guns, would not be affected.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to gun violence, since the bill removes from future sale the most commonly cited weapons in mass shootings — military-style semiautomatic rifles and pistols and magazines over 10 rounds. Current owners keep their weapons, so nobody loses a gun they already have.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess a semiautomatic assault weapon, defined by features such as a detachable magazine plus a pistol grip, folding stock, threaded barrel, or barrel shroud, and by a long named list of AK, AR-15, Uzi, and similar models [S2] [S3].
Makes it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess large-capacity ammunition feeding devices holding more than 10 rounds [S2].

Lets people who lawfully owned these weapons keep them; grandfathered assault weapons must be stored securely and private sales or transfers must go through a licensed dealer with a background check, while grandfathered large magazines can be kept but not resold [S2].

Exempts manually operated bolt, pump, lever, and slide-action guns, antiques, police and retired officers, and a lengthy list of named hunting and sporting rifles and shotguns in Appendix A, so most hunting and target firearms are untouched [S2] [S3].

Requires law enforcement to be notified when a prohibited person tries to buy a grandfathered assault weapon, and lets states use existing Justice Assistance Grant funds to run buy-back programs paying people to surrender these weapons [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers and dealers of the banned rifles, pistols, and large-capacity magazines lose a legal market, and gun buyers who want one of these firearms in the future can no longer buy one new. Existing owners face storage requirements and can no longer sell their guns privately without a dealer and a background check.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and future buyers

drawbacks.text: The ban is defined by features, so it covers a very broad class of firearms — many semiautomatic rifles and pistols with ordinary attachments like a threaded barrel or a forward grip — that millions of Americans lawfully own for sport and self-defense, which is the core objection gun-rights groups and many lawmakers raised [S2] [S3].

Because the bill grandfathers every weapon and magazine already owned, it leaves the existing stock untouched and would only reduce availability gradually as guns age out, so its near-term effect on gun violence is limited [S2].

Appendix A exempts hundreds of hunting and sporting rifles and shotguns, some functionally similar in firepower to listed weapons, a carve-out critics could point to as arbitrary and an opening for manufacturers to redesign around the ban [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a specific class of weapons associated with high-casualty shootings while leaving existing owners, hunters, and sporting shooters whole, so the burden falls mainly on future sales and on the industry. The honest tradeoffs are that a feature-based ban sweeps in some ordinary firearms, and grandfathering means the benefits arrive slowly rather than immediately.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee, where it stayed; there was no committee vote and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Cicilline introduced the bill on December 16, 2015, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
On January 15, 2016, it was referred to the subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill gathered 149 cosponsors, every one of them a Democrat, with no Republican support [S4].
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms manufacturers and dealers who sell semiautomatic rifles, pistols, and high-capacity magazines kept an unrestricted market, and existing owners kept their weapons with no new storage or transfer rules. People hoping for a federal restriction on these weapons got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, sellers, and current owners

for.name: Rep. David Cicilline
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Assault Weapons Ban of 2015 in the House.

for.name: 149 of 188 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a large bloc of support but far short of a House majority.

against.name: Chair Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the committee for a markup or vote; it stayed at the subcommittee level until the Congress ended.

against.name: Speaker Paul Ryan
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote in the Republican-led House.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed renewing or expanding a federal assault weapons ban and pressed House Republicans against it.

sides.party_line_note: All 149 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican backed the bill; the Republican chair of the Judiciary Committee and the Republican speaker never allowed it a vote.

industries.note: The bill criminalizes manufacturing the AR-15, AK-type, and similar semiautomatic weapons named in its definitions, removing their largest product category from the legal market. Their future sales depend on the weapons the bill targets, so their interest runs against the public-safety purpose of the bill.
New magazines holding more than 10 rounds could no longer be made or sold, and existing ones could be kept but never resold, ending that product line.

They lose sales of newly banned weapons and magazines, but gain a required role: private sales and transfers of grandfathered assault weapons must run through a licensed dealer with a background check.
Hundreds of named hunting, target, and competition rifles and shotguns are expressly exempted in Appendix A, so their products and customers are untouched.
